title: The light of the ten
hook: the Ardas turns to the Guru Granth Sahib, the embodied light of the ten Gurus
tomorrow: The five, the four, the forty

segments.voice: Yesterday: help everywhere, and your line: present in every place. Did you pause at a door and say it? The Ardas has now named all ten Gurus. Today it turns to the one in front of the room. Day six hundred twenty.

At a candlelight vigil, the first candle is lit with a match. After that, no one uses a match again. Each person tips their wick into the flame of the person next to them, and the light moves down the line. By the end there are hundreds of candles, but in a sense there's only ever been one flame, passed along. Sikhs have used an image very like this for more than four hundred years, to describe how the Guruship moved from Guru Nanak to the next Guru and the next. And the Ardas, having named all ten, now says where that flame is today. Today: the light of the ten.
screen: `ONE MATCH, THEN NO MORE.` → `WICK TO FLAME, DOWN THE LINE.` → `HUNDREDS OF CANDLES, ONE FLAME.`

segments.voice: After the tenth Guru, the Ardas continues: dasaan paatshaaheeaan dee jot, sri guru granth sahib ji. The light of the ten masters, the Guru Granth Sahib. Jot means light, a flame, the kind that burns in a lamp. In paraphrase, the line goes on: fixing your mind on its reading and the sight of it, say Waheguru! And here, for the first time in the Ardas, the whole room answers aloud: Waheguru. The idea of one light passing on is old. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the bards Satta and Balwand sang that when Guru Nanak installed Guru Angad, it was the same light and the same way; only the body was changed. Sikhs understand each Guru as carrying the one jot, the one flame, in a new body, ten times. Then in 1708, tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh passed the Guruship not to a person but to the scripture. So the flame that went from candle to candle now burns in a book. That's why Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib not as a book about the Guru, but as the Guru. It rests on a raised seat under a canopy. Someone waves a chaur, a whisk, over it as it's read. At night it's carried to its own room to rest. People bow when they enter its presence. To someone outside, that can look like honoring an object. Sikhs would say it's honoring a presence: the light of all ten, in one place, still speaking. The ten in one. And the Ardas, every time it's prayed, turns toward it.
screen: `JOT: THE LIGHT IN THE LAMP.` · `SAME LIGHT, ONLY THE BODY CHANGED.` · `THE FLAME NOW BURNS IN A BOOK.` · `HONORING A PRESENCE.` · then, large: `THE TEN IN ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a page of the Granth. If you can, open one, in a gurdwara or on a screen; any Ang will do. If not, picture it: the Gurmukhi letters in long lines, the cloth around it, the canopy above. Let your eyes rest on the page without trying to read it all. Just look, the way you'd look at a candle flame. Think of ten lives passing one light down. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, the room's answer, once, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Jot, light, a flame. Dasaan paatshaaheeaan dee jot: one jot, carried by ten Gurus, now burning in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Your line: the ten in one. If you see a candle or a lamp lit today, let it remind you of the flame passed down the line. Day six hundred twenty.

howItsDone: After naming the ten Gurus, the Ardas turns to the Guru Granth Sahib as the light of the ten masters, and the sangat answers Waheguru aloud; Sikhs bow before it and treat it as the living Guru.

fork.setup: you're visiting a gurdwara for the first time and see people bowing to the Guru Granth Sahib. a friend asks why. what would Sikhs say?
options: it's a very old and valuable book.
it's the Guru: the light of the ten, still present.
it's a custom with no meaning.
fork.reveal: Sikhs honor a presence, not an object: the one jot that passed through ten Gurus now burns in the scripture.

original.note: Gurmukhi: jot, light or flame; the Ardas calls the Guru Granth Sahib the light of the ten masters.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Granth is honored because it's holy writing.
what it means: it's honored as the Guru, the one light that passed through ten Gurus.
what a scholar hears: Satta and Balwand's Ramkali vaar (Ang 966) has jot oha jugat sai, sahi kaaiaa pher palatteeai: same light, same way, only the body changed.
recall: a sword; God seen as power
